messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sofia was seven years old the first time she understood that love could smell like fear. She had been hiding under the kitchen table, her small hands pressed over her ears, but she could still hear her father’s voice rising and falling like a storm, and her mother’s quieter, broken sounds. What she remembered most vividly now, at thirty-nine, was not the shouting itself but the air—thick with the sharp, metallic tang of her father’s sweat as he loomed over her mother, and the way that smell seemed to cling to everything for days afterward. When she tried to deliberately recall the details of that night, the memory was stubbornly fragmented, slipping away like water through her fingers, leaving only a series of vivid, silent images: the crack in the linoleum floor, the blue of her mother’s housecoat, the way the light from the television flickered across the wall. What came easiest was the grief—a wave of it that would crash over her without warning, so heavy and complete that she sometimes felt she was drowning in the sorrow of a child she no longer was.

Sofia became a detective because she believed that if she could understand the worst of what people did to each other, she could keep herself safe. But the job had only deepened the certainty that had taken root under that kitchen table: that the world was a place where danger could erupt from the most ordinary moments, and that she was the sort of person who attracted it. The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, she had come to believe, a conviction that settled into her bones like a low-grade fever. She had begun to doubt her own instincts—how could she trust that she would do the right thing when she had not been able to protect her mother, had not even known how to run? Her reactions since that night felt like proof that she was going crazy: the way her heart would hammer at the sound of a raised voice in the precinct bullpen, the way she would freeze when a suspect’s sweat-soaked shirt was bagged as evidence, the way she flinched when a colleague clapped a hand on her shoulder in congratulation.

These triggers—the shout, the smell, the touch—did not merely startle her. They sent her spiraling into a state of raw, animal alertness. She would wake in the middle of the night, her body rigid, scanning the darkness of her bedroom for threats that were not there. At work, she always chose her desk with her back to the wall, and in meetings she sat closest to the door, her eyes tracking every movement in the room. An unexpected movement nearby—a detective rising quickly from his chair, a door swinging open too fast—would make her react as if she were already under attack, her hand going to her hip where her service weapon rested. The world had become a series of ambushes waiting to happen, and she was always, always on watch.

The only way Sofia had found to stop the cascade was to hurt herself. When the images of her mother’s face, pale and streaked with tears, pressed too insistently into her mind, or when the grief threatened to pull her under, she would dig her fingernails into her forearm until the pain cut through the memory. The physical sensation was the only thing that could anchor her back in the present, a harsh reset that silenced the loop of shame and fear. But this strategy came at a cost. The more she relied on it, the more she avoided anything that might stir an emotion at all—she stopped answering calls from her sister, stopped watching movies with her partner, stopped letting herself feel anything that could tip into either joy or despair. She had learned to hold herself still, emotionally and physically, bracing against contact. She avoided being touched with a vigilance that her partner had begun to notice and, quietly, to resent. When he reached for her in bed, she would go stiff, and the look on his face—hurt, confused—only confirmed her belief that she was broken, that she could not do anything right.

The memories, when they came, were not something she chose. They arrived as unbidden pictures, and each one brought with it the old grief and the old accusation: this happened because of who you are. That belief, in turn, made her more sensitive to the triggers around her—a man’s laugh in a coffee shop, the smell of sweat on a crowded subway car—so that she was constantly scanning, constantly waiting for the next assault on her senses. And each time she flinched or froze or hurt herself to escape, she proved to herself again that she was not in control, that she was, in fact, going crazy. The cycle tightened until her whole life had become a series of small, invisible battles fought in the space between one breath and the next.

What finally brought Sofia to seek help was not the fear or the grief or the shame. It was the morning she found herself standing in her own kitchen, unable to move, because her partner had set a glass down too hard on the counter. The sound had sent her somewhere else entirely, and when she came back, he was staring at her with a look she recognized—it was the same look her mother had worn, years ago, after the shouting had stopped and the air had gone quiet. Sofia knew then that she was losing not just her peace of mind, but the life she had tried so hard to build. She was terrified that if she did not change something, she would end up alone, trapped in the same silence she had sworn she would never repeat. She did not know if she could trust herself to get better, but she knew she could not keep going the way she was.
